notes: Patterns are case-insensitive. Each match is exactly the span to replace (context sits in lookarounds); replace it with `right`, matching the case of the first letter, unless `rule` or `risk` says otherwise. `harper_rule` names an existing Harper rule (default_config.json, enabled by default) that covers the same error.

items.wrong: could of / should of / would of
items.right: could have / should have / would have
items.rule: after could/should/would (or their n't forms) or "ought to", except before "course"; replace only "of" with "have"
items.why: Spoken "could've" is pronounced like "could of", and Whisper's web-text training data contains the misspelling. Never standard English.
items.risk: "of course" is excluded. No other standard sequence exists.

items.rule: replace only "of"; except before "course" or after "the"/"a" (wine "must")
items.risk: Winemaking noun "the must of the grapes" is excluded by the lookbehind.

items.rule: after a subject pronoun + might/may; replace only "of"; except before "course"
items.why: Spoken "might've" and "may've" sound like "might of" and "may of". A pronoun subject is required because "the might of Rome" and "in May of 2026" are standard.
items.risk: Noun "might" and the month "May" never follow a subject pronoun directly.

items.why: The final /d/ of "supposed" merges into the /t/ of "to", so engines often drop it. A test post using Word's dictation shows the same tense-ending loss ("pass down" for "passed down").
items.risk: Harper's SupposedTo flags every "suppose to", including "I suppose to some degree"; Verbose's version requires a preceding "be".

items.why: D-elision: "used to" is pronounced /juːstə/, identical to "use to".
items.risk: "of use to" is not matched (the word before is "of").

items.why: Homophone; "past" and "passed" are pronounced the same.
items.risk: none

items.rule: after an auxiliary or subject pronoun
items.risk: "walked past away fans" is not matched because the word before is a verb.
Soccer "own goal" ("was there an own goal") needs "an" in between, so it is not matched.

items.rule: at sentence start before a form of "be", or after "is/are" before a/any/anything
items.why: Homophone; "their" cannot be a sentence subject before "is".
items.risk: none

items.why: Homophone. Can't be fixed blind: "there" is valid in "is there money".
items.risk: Questions ("is there work today") use "there" before a noun.

items.why: Homophone. "Are there going to be" is valid, so it can't be auto-fixed.
items.risk: "Are there going to be problems?" uses "there".

items.rule: at the end of a clause, not after "for" or "warm"
items.risk: "Thanks for your welcome." is excluded by the lookbehind.
none

items.why: Homophone. "your right hand" and "your going-away party" are valid.
items.risk: Noun uses ("your right to vote") are common.

items.why: Homophone; only the possessive precedes "own". (The reverse, "its" before a verb, is already in Verbose's Harper pass.)
items.risk: none

items.rule: a standalone reply: "me to" or "me two" alone in its sentence
items.why: to/too/two substitutions appear in LibriSpeech confusion pairs (to==>too, too==>to, two==>too). Replace the matched phrase with "me too" (or "you too").
items.risk: "...and you to." can be elliptical ("I asked him and you to."), which is rare in dictation.

items.why: LibriSpeech confusion pairs include two==>too; "two much" is never standard.
items.risk: "two many-sided shapes" is excluded by the hyphen check.

items.why: Documented to==>too confusion, but "from early to late" and "from bad to worse" are valid.
items.risk: Range phrases ("from hot to cold").

items.why: then/than reduce to the same unstressed vowel /ðən/.
items.risk: none

items.wrong: and than / since than / until than
items.right: and then / since then / until then
items.why: Same reduced vowel. "than" cannot follow a conjunction or these prepositions.
items.risk: "back than" is deliberately left out ("I'd rather go back than stay").

items.why: Common confusion, but dictation often lacks commas: "once more then stop", "see each other then".
items.risk: Missing commas make "then" valid in many cases.

items.wrong: side affect / take affect / an affect on
items.rule: in fixed noun contexts; replace "affect" with "effect" (keep any plural "s")
patterns: (?<=\b(?:take|takes|took|taken|taking|come into|came into|comes into|go into|goes into|went into|put into) )affect\b
items.why: Near-homophone (/əˈfɛkt/ vs /ɪˈfɛkt/ collapse in fast speech).
items.risk: Psychology uses "affect" as a noun ("flat affect"); "the/positive/negative affect" and bare "side affects" ("one side affects the other") are deliberately not matched.

items.rule: after a modal or negation, before an object pronoun
items.why: Near-homophone; the verb "effect" (bring about) never takes a person as object.
items.risk: "her" is excluded because "effect her release" is valid.

items.rule: after a subject or modal, before an acceptable thing
items.risk: "everything except the offer" is excluded because "everything" is not in the lookbehind list.
none

items.wrong: backhanded complement / complements of the chef
items.rule: in fixed phrases; replace "complement" with "compliment" (keep any plural "s")
items.risk: none
none
none
"we hit a peak at noon" is not matched.
"interest rates peaked" has a different word order and is not matched.

items.rule: before possessive + common object, or after to/can/will before "weight"
items.why: Near-homophone; ASR and writers both confuse /luːz/ and /luːs/.
items.risk: "let loose her hair" is excluded; "hair" and "grip" are left out.
none

items.wrong: break pedal / slam on the breaks
items.risk: "break lines" is left out ("break lines at 80 characters").
"spring brake" (truck part) is deliberately excluded.

items.why: Classic mondegreen; the spoken form is near-identical.
items.risk: none

items.rule: after a form of "be", at clause end
items.why: "and" reduces to /ən/, heard as "in" (LibriSpeech and==>in is the 4th most common substitution).
items.risk: "we have one in the same color" is excluded by the "be" and clause-end requirements.

items.rule: after a/perfect/classic, or alone before punctuation
items.why: and/in reduce to the same vowel.
items.risk: "make the case and point out" is excluded.
none
none

items.wrong: bare with me / bare in mind
items.right: bear with me / bear in mind
items.rule: before with + pronoun, or before "in mind"
items.risk: Only "me"/"us" after "with" to avoid "left bare with them".
none

items.rule: after "free", or reign + object + "in"; replace the stem "reign" with "rein" and keep any suffix
items.risk: "his reign in England" is not matched.

"$10 per, say, 5 units" without commas is rare.

items.why: Near-homophone; match is the stem, keep the suffix.
items.risk: none

items.rule: always ("a piece of my mind" has "my" and is not matched)
items.risk: none

items.rule: after a negation, before an object pronoun, not before out/in
items.why: Exact homophones. Match is "phase"; replace with "faze" and keep a following "d".
items.risk: "we won't phase them out" is excluded.
Passive "eluded to capture" is rare.

items.why: Nonstandard variant; "a" and "the" are the most confused pair in ASR.
items.risk: Some users say "all of the sudden" on purpose.

items.rule: before going/coming/ready/in charge, not a hyphen
items.risk: "whose going-away party" is excluded.
"the pipe has lead to the valve" (metal) is very rare.

items.why: Not a standard word; appears in web text that Whisper learned from.
items.risk: none

items.rule: at the end of a clause, not after a degree word
items.why: Spoken identically; only the adverb ends a clause.
items.risk: Predicative adjective ("it's so everyday") is excluded.

items.rule: after a determiner, before a noun
items.why: Spoken identically. A preceding determiner forces the adjective reading.
items.risk: Sentence-initial "Every day life gets harder" is not matched because it may mean "Every day, life...".
none. Note: Harper's closed-compound rule "Everyone" flags "every one" everywhere, including the correct "every one of them"; don't auto-apply it.

items.why: Spoken identically; "awhile" already means "for a while".
items.risk: none

items.rule: after a subject, before a determiner or common adjective
items.why: Spoken identically; a subject followed by a predicate needs the verb.
items.risk: Colloquial "I maybe a little" is uncommon; "there's maybe a dozen" is not matched ("there's").

items.rule: at sentence start before a pronoun or time word
items.risk: Labels like "May be subject to change" are excluded by the word list.

items.right: set up / log in / back up
items.rule: after a modal, "how to", or "need to"
items.why: Phrasal verb and noun are spoken alike; engines pick the noun spelling learned from software text. Replace with the two-word verb (setup→set up, login→log in, backup→back up, signup→sign up, logout→log out, checkout→check out, workout→work out, shutdown→shut down, lookup→look up).
items.risk: Noun after "how to" is rare ("how to backup software works").

items.rule: before a pronoun, determiner, or conjunction
items.why: Documented ASR substitution: an==>and and and==>an are top-30 confusion pairs on LibriSpeech test-other. Harper's a/an rule may then turn this "an" into "a", so run this fix before Harper.
items.risk: "an his" is not standard in American English ("an historic" is a different word). Harper's AnA rule conflicts: it may rewrite "an the" as "a the". Apply this fix before Harper runs.

items.rule: after a subject or do-auxiliary, before a wh-word or "that"
items.why: Exact homophones; LibriSpeech confusion pairs include know==>no.
items.risk: "I no longer" and "to no avail" are not matched.

items.rule: after can/did/could you or a subject, before a pronoun or "about"
items.why: Exact homophones; LibriSpeech confusion pairs include here==>hear and hear==>here.
items.risk: "We here at Acme" is not matched ("at" is not in the list).

items.rule: two identical function words in a row; delete the second
items.why: Engines transcribe stutters and restarts verbatim; Whisper also repeats tokens when decoding loops.
items.risk: "had had", "that that", and "is is" are valid and left out. Replace the whole match with the single word.

items.rule: digits with the wrong suffix; recompute the suffix
items.why: Inverse text normalization can join a digit to a spoken suffix inconsistently. The correct suffix is deterministic from the digits.
items.risk: none

items.rule: a dollar sign plus the word "dollars"; delete " dollars"
items.why: Whisper writes the currency symbol for spoken "dollars"; when it also keeps the word, the result is redundant. Whisper's own normalizer maps "dollars" to "$".
items.risk: The match is " dollars" (with its leading space); delete it. "5 dollars" without a symbol is untouched.

items.why: Plural decades take no apostrophe; but "the 1990's biggest hit" is a possessive.
items.risk: Possessive use.
